cards.text: Isaiah, the prophet, has another burden, and this one is against Dumah. He says a voice calls out to him, crying for the watchman. Somebody out there needs an answer.

cards.question: In the burden against Dumah, where does that voice calling for the watchman come from?
The voice from Seir calls to the watchman, the one keeping guard while everyone else sleeps. What does it want to know?

answers.text: How much of the night is left
Who is coming up the road
Whether the city is still safe

cards.text: "Watchman, what is left of the night?" Friend, I spent YEARS in the dark in a junk drawer, and nobody could tell me that, because the dead batteries I shared that drawer with were too busy arguing about who had the most charge left.

cards.question: The voice from Seir asks the watchman how much of the night is left only one time.

cards.text: Now the watchman answers. And it is NOT the kind of answer you can text back with a thumbs up.

cards.question: The watchman's answer is all good news: morning has come and the night is over.

cards.text: Morning has come, but also the night, like a weather app calling for sunshine AND storms in the same hour. But the watchman isn't done talking.

cards.question: The watchman doesn't send the caller away. He says if the caller wants to ___, then go ahead, and come back yet again.

cards.text: And that's the whole burden: a voice in the dark, an answer with morning and night in it, and a watchman telling the caller to come back yet again. Two verses, friend, and somehow it STILL keeps you up at night.

findings.problem: The card says the voice is 'crying for the watchman.' The BSB says 'One calls to me,' so 'calls' is the text's word. 'Crying' adds an emotional tone the text doesn't give.

rule.text: Call things what the text calls them.

findings.problem: This story card only re-quotes the question from Isaiah 21:11, which card 3 already covered, and adds a joke. It doesn't carry the passage to a new moment, so it works as a recap card.

The setup line says the watchman's reply 'is NOT the kind of answer you can text back with a thumbs up.' That rules out 'True' on card 7, which asks whether the answer is all good news, so card 6 gives the answer away.

rule.text: A setup line can't rule out the wrong answers either.

findings.problem: The last story card sums up the whole passage: the voice, the morning and night answer, and the call to come back again. All of that has already been told or asked, so this is a recap card, not a card that moves the passage forward.
The card cites Isaiah 21:12, but it retells content from both verses, including the voice from 21:11. Its citation is narrower than what it uses.

rule.text: Every story card cites the verses it tells, from the first verse it uses to the last, no wider and no narrower.
